screens.title: Monitoring Fabric Networks: Tools and Metrics
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring is the live pulse of a production Fabric network. In this lesson you will learn why continuous metric collection matters, which Fabric metrics give you early warning of problems, and how Prometheus and Grafana work together to collect and surface that data. We will illustrate concrete examples: detecting a peer that lags in block height, spotting chaincode latency spikes, and using alerts to notify operators before outages escalate. You will also follow a short, practical walkthrough that starts the test network with Prometheus enabled, verifies metrics endpoints, and imports a Fabric dashboard into Grafana. A common misconception is that dashboards alone are sufficient — in practice dashboards need well-chosen metrics, tuned alerts, and historical baselines to be reliable. By the end of this lesson you will know what to monitor, how to wire Fabric components into Prometheus, and how to design a dashboard that reveals system health at a glance. Consider how an alert for a lagging peer would change your on-call workflow and what immediate checks you would run.

screens.title: What is monitoring for Fabric?
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring for Fabric is the continuous cycle of collecting metrics, analyzing them, and presenting them so operators can make timely decisions. Practically, monitoring gathers quantifiable signals from peers, orderers, chaincode, and supporting services and turns them into graphs, alerts, and reports. Think of it as a heart-rate monitor for your blockchain: block height, transaction throughput, and latency are vital signs. A concrete example: tracking peer block height across organizations lets you detect ledger synchronization issues early — if one peer falls behind, queries and endorsements may become inconsistent. A common misconception is that capturing a large number of metrics alone will guarantee observability. In reality, you must choose relevant metrics, retain historical data to build baselines, and create meaningful alerts that minimize noise. Another mistake is relying solely on dashboards without alerting — dashboards are great for exploration, but alerts notify you when something crosses a threshold so you can act immediately. Key takeaways: define what matters to your network, collect those metrics consistently, and use both visualization and alerting to close the loop between detection and remediation. How would you prioritize which Fabric metric to monitor first for your production network?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › What is monitoring for Fabric?
Definition & scope

Monitoring gathers telemetry from Fabric components and supporting services, analyzes trends, and surfaces actionable insights through dashboards and alerts.

Analogy
Like a heart monitor for a system: track vital signs to detect anomalies early.
Common misconception
More metrics does not equal more visibility; choose relevant metrics and keep history for baselines.
Why it matters
Early detection prevents inconsistency, reduces downtime, and speeds incident response.
Operational example: block height lag
If one peer's block height is behind its peers on the same channel, it indicates a synchronization problem that can affect queries and endorsements.
Signal
fabric_peer_ledger_height_total
Compare this metric across peers to detect lag.
Action
Check peer logs, network connectivity, database errors, and resource utilization.
Key takeaway
Monitoring is useful only when metrics are chosen for impact, historical context is retained, and alerts are meaningful.

screens.title: Peer metrics you must monitor
screens.narratorSegment: Peers are the backbone of Fabric ledger replication and endorsement. Monitoring peer metrics gives you insight into consensus, data freshness, and performance. Important peer metrics include block height — the everyday way to check ledger synchronization; transaction rate — how many transactions are committed per second; endorsement latency — how long a peer takes to endorse; state database size — growth of CouchDB or LevelDB; resource utilization — C P U, memory, and disk input and output; gossip messages — counts and active connections; and chaincode container health — status and resource usage of the execution environment. A concrete example: imagine your Grafana dashboard shows that one peer's C P U is pegged while its block height falls behind. This suggests either resource contention or a heavy chaincode causing slow processing. A common misconception is to treat gossip message counts as noise; in fact sudden drops or spikes often indicate network partitioning or peer disconnection. Operationally, use peer metrics together: pair ledger height with resource metrics and gossip stats to form a diagnosis. The immediate steps for a lagging peer are to check peer logs for gossip or database errors, verify connectivity to peers and orderers, and inspect the state database size. What combination of metrics would you inspect first when a peer's endorsements begin to fail?

keyIdea.title: Peer health checklist
keyIdea.text: Monitor ledger height, transaction throughput, endorsement latency, state DB growth, gossip activity, and resource usage to detect peer-level issues.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Peer metrics you must monitor
Peer metric list
  • Block Height: ledger block number; compare peers to detect sync issues.
  • Transaction Rate: committed transactions per second; spikes reveal load changes.
  • Endorsement Latency: time to endorse; affects transaction latency and throughput.
  • State DB Size: CouchDB/LevelDB growth impacts disk I/O and compaction times.
  • Gossip Messages: message counts and connection counts reflect peer mesh health.
  • Chaincode Container Health: container status and resource usage indicate execution problems.
Diagnostic example
Scenario: Peer A's block height lags behind Peer B. Combine three checks to diagnose quickly.
Metric
fabric_peer_ledger_height_total
Compare across peers on the same channel.
Resource
CPU, memory, disk I/O
Use docker stats or cloud metrics for the peer process.
Network
Gossip messages and connection counts
Drop in messages may indicate partitioning.
Key Takeaway

Use a combination of ledger, resource, and gossip metrics to form a reliable hypothesis about peer issues before remediation.

screens.title: Orderer metrics and consensus visibility
screens.narratorSegment: Orderers are responsible for ordering transactions into blocks, so watching orderer metrics gives you visibility into throughput, leader stability, and potential bottlenecks. Key orderer metrics include block creation rate, which shows how frequently new blocks are cut; transaction queue size, indicating backlog waiting to be ordered; consensus state, such as leader status and follower synchronization in a Raft cluster; and orderer resource utilization. For example, if the block creation rate drops while the transaction queue grows, that signals the orderer cannot keep up — perhaps due to C P U exhaustion or a consensus stall. A misconception is to assume only peers must be monitored. In multi-node networks the orderer is a single point of coordination; leader changes or synchronization issues will affect all peers when blocks stop being created. To diagnose, check Raft leader metrics, follower replication lag, and orderer logs for consensus errors. Design alerts that detect when the orderer is not producing blocks or when leader elections take longer than expected. These alerts should carry context: which channel is affected, current queue size, and whether the cluster has a stable leader. What would you prioritize alerting for in a production orderer cluster?

keyIdea.title: Orderer observability
keyIdea.text: Track block creation, transaction queues, consensus leader state, and orderer resource usage to detect ordering or consensus failures early.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Orderer metrics and consensus visibility
Important orderer metrics
  • Block Creation Rate: how often blocks are cut for channels.
  • Transaction Queue Size: transactions waiting to be ordered.
  • Consensus State: leader status, follower synchronization in Raft.
  • Resource Utilization: CPU, memory, and disk I/O for the orderer process.
Operational hint
Alert on sustained queue growth and block creation stalls rather than transient dips to avoid noise.
Consensus scenario
If a Raft leader steps down and followers do not elect a new leader quickly, block creation can stop across channels.
Signal
raft_leader_changes_total
Track leader churn and election delays.
Action
Check orderer logs for election errors, verify network connectivity between Raft nodes, and inspect resource metrics.
Key Takeaway

Orderer-level alerts should track both throughput and consensus health to avoid broad outages caused by leader instability.

screens.title: Chaincode metrics: latency, invocations, and errors
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode metrics tell you how smart contracts are performing from the user's perspective. Key signals include invocation count or rate — how often functions are called; execution latency — how long functions take to run; and error rate — how often executions fail. A concrete example is monitoring the createAsset function: counting invocations shows usage, measuring average execution latency shows performance, and tracking errors reveals reliability issues. To calculate average latency you can use counters for total duration and calls and divide the rates, or use histogram metrics and histogram quantiles for a more accurate view. A common mistake is relying only on averages; averages can hide high tail latencies. Use percentiles or histogram-based quantiles to understand the distribution of execution times. When you see increasing execution latency, investigate chaincode logic complexity, state database access patterns, and chaincode container resource limits. A final tip: tag metrics with the function name to write focused alerts, for example an alert for createAsset average latency above 500 milliseconds. How would you detect a sudden regression in a chaincode function after a new deployment?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Chaincode metrics
Metrics to collect
  • Invocation Count/Rate: per-function call frequency.
  • Execution Latency: measured per function, prefer histograms for percentiles.
  • Error Rate: failed executions per unit time.
Best practice
Use function labels on metrics so you can write alerts specific to a hot or failing function.
Concrete example
To alert on high average latency for createAsset, compute average duration over five minutes by dividing the rate of duration sum by the rate of count. Prefer histograms for precise percentiles if available.
# Example metric names
fabric_chaincode_function_duration_seconds_sum{function="createAsset"}
fabric_chaincode_function_duration_seconds_count{function="createAsset"}
Common mistake

Relying on averages hides tail latency. Use histograms or percentiles when possible to detect user-impacting slow executions.

screens.title: Enable Prometheus metrics on Fabric components
screens.narratorSegment: Enabling Prometheus on Fabric components is a configuration step followed by verification. You enable metrics by setting the metrics provider environment variable on each component: set the peer provider to Prometheus, set the orderer provider to Prometheus, and set the CA provider similarly. Once enabled, each component exposes an HTTP metrics endpoint where Prometheus can scrape numeric samples. For example, set the peer variable CORE_METRICS_PROVIDER to the value that enables Prometheus; similarly set ORDERER_METRICS_PROVIDER for orderers. After restart, verify the endpoints by curling the metrics path for a peer or an orderer and observing Prometheus formatted output. Then configure Prometheus with scrape targets using static_configs or Kubernetes service discovery depending on your deployment. A common misconfiguration is incorrect target addresses or blocked ports; ensure firewalls and port mappings allow Prometheus to reach the endpoints. Finally, keep a consistent naming scheme and labels so you can write targeted PromQL queries. Practice: enable metrics, curl the endpoint to confirm output, and then add the target to Prometheus and confirm scrape success in the Prometheus UI. Enable Prometheus metrics on Fabric components means set the fabric metrics provider env vars, restart components, verify endpoints with curl, and add scrape targets in prometheus using static configs or service discovery.. In practical terms, environment variables, endpoints, and scrape configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Set the Fabric metrics provider env vars, restart components, verify endpoints with curl, and add scrape targets in Prometheus using static configs or service discovery.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Enable Prometheus metrics
Configuration steps
  1. Set CORE_METRICS_PROVIDER=prometheus for peers.
  2. Set ORDERER_METRICS_PROVIDER=prometheus for orderers.
  3. Set FABRIC_CA_SERVER_METRICS_PROVIDER=prometheus for CAs.
  4. Restart components and confirm HTTP /metrics endpoints are available.
  5. Add targets to Prometheus via static_configs or service discovery and reload Prometheus.
Remember to open or map the metrics ports and check network policies if Prometheus cannot scrape.
Verification example
After enabling metrics, run a simple curl against the peer's metrics endpoint and expect a Prometheus-style output of metric names and numeric samples.
# Example environment variables to set
CORE_METRICS_PROVIDER=prometheus
ORDERER_METRICS_PROVIDER=prometheus
FABRIC_CA_SERVER_METRICS_PROVIDER=prometheus

# Example Prometheus static_configs snippet
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'fabric'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['peer0.org1:9051','orderer.example.com:8050']
Key Takeaway

Enable the provider, verify endpoints manually, then add targets in Prometheus and confirm scrapes to close the loop.

screens.title: Prometheus queries and alerting rules
screens.narratorSegment: Prometheus lets you write expressions to compute metrics and to trigger alerts. For latency alerts a practical approach is to divide the rate of the duration sum by the rate of the count over a time window to compute average execution time. The chapter provides an alert example that monitors average latency of a chaincode function and fires if it exceeds 500 milliseconds over five minutes. Use the rate function on counters to produce per-second rates and divide the rates for an average. The alert includes a for clause to avoid transient spikes causing noise. A common misunderstanding is to create alerts with no duration window, which causes flapping. Another mistake is not labeling alerts with instance and function details; include labels and annotations to make alerts actionable. When you test your rule, generate traffic for that function and watch the alert in the Prometheus Alertmanager or your notification channel. Finally, prefer histograms and histogram_quantile for percentile-based alerts when you need to capture tail latency precisely. Which approach would you choose for detecting 99th percentile latency regressions in production? Prometheus queries and alerting rules means compute averages with rate of sum over rate of count for counters, use 'for' to avoid flapping, and annotate alerts with instance and function context.. In practical terms, writing promql and a prometheus alert for chaincode latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Alert design
keyIdea.text: Compute averages with rate of sum over rate of count for counters, use 'for' to avoid flapping, and annotate alerts with instance and function context.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Prometheus queries & alerting
Alerting rule example
Use rates of counters to compute average duration and trigger an alert when average exceeds 0.5 seconds over five minutes.
groups:
- name: fabric_chaincode_alerts
  rules:
  - alert: HighCreateAssetLatency
    expr: |
      rate(fabric_chaincode_function_duration_seconds_sum{function="createAsset"}[5m])
      /
      rate(fabric_chaincode_function_duration_seconds_count{function="createAsset"}[5m])
      > 0.5
    for: 1m
    labels:
      severity: warning
    annotations:
      summary: "High latency for 'createAsset' chaincode function"
      description: "Average execution time for 'createAsset' on instance {{ $labels.instance }} exceeded 500ms for more than 1 minute."
Reading the rule
  • rate(...[5m]) computes per-second rate over five minutes.
  • Divide sum by count to get average duration per call.
  • for: 1m avoids firing on short spikes.

screens.title: Troubleshooting a lagging peer — investigative steps
screens.narratorSegment: When you observe a peer lagging in block height, follow a focused investigative procedure. First, check the peer logs for errors from gossip, committer, or database modules; look for warnings about failed state updates or connection errors. Second, verify network connectivity between the lagging peer, other peers, and the orderer — ensure required ports are reachable and there is no packet loss or firewall blocking. Third, inspect resource utilization for the peer process and its state database; high C P U, memory pressure, or disk input and output can slow block processing. Fourth, verify orderer health and block creation rate since a stalled orderer can make peers appear lagging. A practical step sequence: collect peer logs around the time of lag, run docker stats or cloud metrics for the peer and CouchDB containers, test TCP connectivity to peers and orderer, and consult Prometheus metrics for gossip message counts and ledger height differences. A common misconception is to immediately restart the peer; while restart can help, it risks hiding root causes if you do not gather logs and metrics first. End with a hypothesis and a remediation plan based on observed signals. After running these steps, what evidence would confirm the cause was network partitioning versus resource exhaustion?

screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Operators commonly fall into a few traps when building observability for Fabric. One is not enabling metrics at all by forgetting to set the metrics provider environment variables; without metrics you are blind. Another is incorrect Prometheus configuration: wrong target addresses, blocked ports, or misconfigured service discovery prevent scrapes. Dashboards can become overly complex and noisy, making it hard to find critical signals; prioritize the most important panels. Alerts are often too noisy or too silent — either they fire on harmless transient spikes or they miss true failures because thresholds are set without baselining. A best practice is to establish normal baselines from historical data, tune alert windows and thresholds, and use a small set of well-labeled, high-signal alerts for on-call. Retain historical metrics long enough to analyze trends and gradual degradation. Finally, use labels consistently across metrics so PromQL queries are reliable. A helpful exercise is to audit your dashboards and alerts: remove low-value panels, define three on-call alerts with clear runbook steps, and verify metrics endpoints are scraped. Which of these practices would you implement first on your network?

fullNarratorScript:
Monitoring is the live pulse of a production Fabric network. In this lesson you will learn why continuous metric collection matters, which Fabric metrics give you early warning of problems, and how Prometheus and Grafana work together to collect and surface that data. We will illustrate concrete examples: detecting a peer that lags in block height, spotting chaincode latency spikes, and using alerts to notify operators before outages escalate. You will also follow a short, practical walkthrough that starts the test network with Prometheus enabled, verifies metrics endpoints, and imports a Fabric dashboard into Grafana. A common misconception is that dashboards alone are sufficient — in practice dashboards need well-chosen metrics, tuned alerts, and historical baselines to be reliable. By the end of this lesson you will know what to monitor, how to wire Fabric components into Prometheus, and how to design a dashboard that reveals system health at a glance. Consider how an alert for a lagging peer would change your on-call workflow and what immediate checks you would run.

In this chapter you will build practical skills so you can operate a Hyperledger Fabric network with visibility and confidence. First, you will learn why continuous monitoring is essential and how missing telemetry creates operational blind spots. Then you will identify specific metrics to track for peers, orderers, and chaincode and understand how those metrics map to real symptoms like ledger lag or high latency. Next, you'll configure Fabric components to expose Prometheus-format metrics and wire Prometheus to scrape those endpoints. Finally, you will design Grafana dashboards and alerts so you can both see problems and be notified when thresholds are crossed. Each objective ties back to a hands-on action: enabling metrics, verifying endpoints, importing dashboards, and writing an alerting rule. These skills help you reduce mean time to detection and mean time to recovery in production. Consider how being able to spot a lagging peer quickly would change your incident response steps.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied practice and assessment. You will be able to start the Fabric test network with Prometheus enabled, verify that peer and orderer metrics endpoints return Prometheus-formatted metrics, and import a community Fabric dashboard into Grafana. You will learn to craft a Prometheus alerting rule for a specific chaincode latency condition and to interpret what a lagging block height across peers implies for ledger synchronization. Each objective ends with a short verification step: run a curl against the metrics endpoint, run a Prometheus expression to surface a metric value, and change an alert threshold to observe firing. A common misconception is to set alert thresholds without first establishing a baseline; you will practice using historical metrics to choose meaningful thresholds. Completing these tasks prepares you to pass an operational assessment and to run production monitoring with confidence.

Monitoring for Fabric is the continuous cycle of collecting metrics, analyzing them, and presenting them so operators can make timely decisions. Practically, monitoring gathers quantifiable signals from peers, orderers, chaincode, and supporting services and turns them into graphs, alerts, and reports. Think of it as a heart-rate monitor for your blockchain: block height, transaction throughput, and latency are vital signs. A concrete example: tracking peer block height across organizations lets you detect ledger synchronization issues early — if one peer falls behind, queries and endorsements may become inconsistent. A common misconception is that capturing a large number of metrics alone will guarantee observability. In reality, you must choose relevant metrics, retain historical data to build baselines, and create meaningful alerts that minimize noise. Another mistake is relying solely on dashboards without alerting — dashboards are great for exploration, but alerts notify you when something crosses a threshold so you can act immediately. Key takeaways: define what matters to your network, collect those metrics consistently, and use both visualization and alerting to close the loop between detection and remediation. How would you prioritize which Fabric metric to monitor first for your production network?

Peers are the backbone of Fabric ledger replication and endorsement. Monitoring peer metrics gives you insight into consensus, data freshness, and performance. Important peer metrics include block height — the everyday way to check ledger synchronization; transaction rate — how many transactions are committed per second; endorsement latency — how long a peer takes to endorse; state database size — growth of CouchDB or LevelDB; resource utilization — C P U, memory, and disk input and output; gossip messages — counts and active connections; and chaincode container health — status and resource usage of the execution environment. A concrete example: imagine your Grafana dashboard shows that one peer's C P U is pegged while its block height falls behind. This suggests either resource contention or a heavy chaincode causing slow processing. A common misconception is to treat gossip message counts as noise; in fact sudden drops or spikes often indicate network partitioning or peer disconnection. Operationally, use peer metrics together: pair ledger height with resource metrics and gossip stats to form a diagnosis. The immediate steps for a lagging peer are to check peer logs for gossip or database errors, verify connectivity to peers and orderers, and inspect the state database size. What combination of metrics would you inspect first when a peer's endorsements begin to fail?

Orderers are responsible for ordering transactions into blocks, so watching orderer metrics gives you visibility into throughput, leader stability, and potential bottlenecks. Key orderer metrics include block creation rate, which shows how frequently new blocks are cut; transaction queue size, indicating backlog waiting to be ordered; consensus state, such as leader status and follower synchronization in a Raft cluster; and orderer resource utilization. For example, if the block creation rate drops while the transaction queue grows, that signals the orderer cannot keep up — perhaps due to C P U exhaustion or a consensus stall. A misconception is to assume only peers must be monitored. In multi-node networks the orderer is a single point of coordination; leader changes or synchronization issues will affect all peers when blocks stop being created. To diagnose, check Raft leader metrics, follower replication lag, and orderer logs for consensus errors. Design alerts that detect when the orderer is not producing blocks or when leader elections take longer than expected. These alerts should carry context: which channel is affected, current queue size, and whether the cluster has a stable leader. What would you prioritize alerting for in a production orderer cluster?

Chaincode metrics tell you how smart contracts are performing from the user's perspective. Key signals include invocation count or rate — how often functions are called; execution latency — how long functions take to run; and error rate — how often executions fail. A concrete example is monitoring the createAsset function: counting invocations shows usage, measuring average execution latency shows performance, and tracking errors reveals reliability issues. To calculate average latency you can use counters for total duration and calls and divide the rates, or use histogram metrics and histogram quantiles for a more accurate view. A common mistake is relying only on averages; averages can hide high tail latencies. Use percentiles or histogram-based quantiles to understand the distribution of execution times. When you see increasing execution latency, investigate chaincode logic complexity, state database access patterns, and chaincode container resource limits. A final tip: tag metrics with the function name to write focused alerts, for example an alert for createAsset average latency above 500 milliseconds. How would you detect a sudden regression in a chaincode function after a new deployment?

Enabling Prometheus on Fabric components is a configuration step followed by verification. You enable metrics by setting the metrics provider environment variable on each component: set the peer provider to Prometheus, set the orderer provider to Prometheus, and set the CA provider similarly. Once enabled, each component exposes an HTTP metrics endpoint where Prometheus can scrape numeric samples. For example, set the peer variable CORE_METRICS_PROVIDER to the value that enables Prometheus; similarly set ORDERER_METRICS_PROVIDER for orderers. After restart, verify the endpoints by curling the metrics path for a peer or an orderer and observing Prometheus formatted output. Then configure Prometheus with scrape targets using static_configs or Kubernetes service discovery depending on your deployment. A common misconfiguration is incorrect target addresses or blocked ports; ensure firewalls and port mappings allow Prometheus to reach the endpoints. Finally, keep a consistent naming scheme and labels so you can write targeted PromQL queries. Practice: enable metrics, curl the endpoint to confirm output, and then add the target to Prometheus and confirm scrape success in the Prometheus UI. Enable Prometheus metrics on Fabric components means set the fabric metrics provider env vars, restart components, verify endpoints with curl, and add scrape targets in prometheus using static configs or service discovery.. In practical terms, environment variables, endpoints, and scrape configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Prometheus lets you write expressions to compute metrics and to trigger alerts. For latency alerts a practical approach is to divide the rate of the duration sum by the rate of the count over a time window to compute average execution time. The chapter provides an alert example that monitors average latency of a chaincode function and fires if it exceeds 500 milliseconds over five minutes. Use the rate function on counters to produce per-second rates and divide the rates for an average. The alert includes a for clause to avoid transient spikes causing noise. A common misunderstanding is to create alerts with no duration window, which causes flapping. Another mistake is not labeling alerts with instance and function details; include labels and annotations to make alerts actionable. When you test your rule, generate traffic for that function and watch the alert in the Prometheus Alertmanager or your notification channel. Finally, prefer histograms and histogram_quantile for percentile-based alerts when you need to capture tail latency precisely. Grafana turns Prometheus metrics into human-friendly dashboards. When you observe a peer lagging in block height, follow a focused investigative procedure. First, check the peer logs for errors from gossip, committer, or database modules; look for warnings about failed state updates or connection errors. Second, verify network connectivity between the lagging peer, other peers, and the orderer — ensure required ports are reachable and there is no packet loss or firewall blocking. Third, inspect resource utilization for the peer process and its state database; high C P U, memory pressure, or disk input and output can slow block processing. Fourth, verify orderer health and block creation rate since a stalled orderer can make peers appear lagging. A practical step sequence: collect peer logs around the time of lag, run docker stats or cloud metrics for the peer and CouchDB containers, test TCP connectivity to peers and orderer, and consult Prometheus metrics for gossip message counts and ledger height differences. A common misconception is to immediately restart the peer; while restart can help, it risks hiding root causes if you do not gather logs and metrics first. End with a hypothesis and a remediation plan based on observed signals. After running these steps, what evidence would confirm the cause was network partitioning versus resource exhaustion?

Operators commonly fall into a few traps when building observability for Fabric. One is not enabling metrics at all by forgetting to set the metrics provider environment variables; without metrics you are blind. Another is incorrect Prometheus configuration: wrong target addresses, blocked ports, or misconfigured service discovery prevent scrapes. Dashboards can become overly complex and noisy, making it hard to find critical signals; prioritize the most important panels. Alerts are often too noisy or too silent — either they fire on harmless transient spikes or they miss true failures because thresholds are set without baselining. A best practice is to establish normal baselines from historical data, tune alert windows and thresholds, and use a small set of well-labeled, high-signal alerts for on-call. Retain historical metrics long enough to analyze trends and gradual degradation. Finally, use labels consistently across metrics so PromQL queries are reliable. A helpful exercise is to audit your dashboards and alerts: remove low-value panels, define three on-call alerts with clear runbook steps, and verify metrics endpoints are scraped. These are the core concepts you should retain: Monitoring is continuous collection, analysis, and visualization of telemetry designed to give operational visibility. Metrics are quantifiable measures such as block height, transaction rate, and chaincode latency that map to symptoms you can act on. Prometheus is the collection layer that scrapes Fabric components and evaluates alerting rules, while Grafana is the visualization layer used to create dashboards and panels. For each concept, remember why it matters and a short example: monitoring prevents surprises, block height comparison reveals ledger sync problems, Prometheus scrapes endpoints to collect numeric metrics, and Grafana panels display those metrics to help operators respond.
